subsubtopic: DRAFT LEGISLATION-MINISTER'S ACCUSATION AGAINST ENVIRONMENTAL LAWYER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has made an unprecedented attack on a Toronto environmental lawyer who criticized his environmental protection draft Bill. In a letter sent to some environment groups, and some members of the news media, the Minister accused Toby Vigod of the Canadian Environmental Law Association of being "factually wrong" when she criticized his draft law.
In an interview, Ms. Vigod and other environmentalists said that they could not recall a federal Environment Minister launching such a public attack on an environmental figure for criticisms of the Minister's work. "He seems very defensive of a Bill which is only a draft Bill," Ms. Vigod said. "We are willing to sit down with him and suggest changes." A spokesman for the Minister said the Minister had offered to meet with Ms. Vigod and that he wanted "to smooth things out".
This temper tantrum by the Minister is pathetic, considering his Government's promises of openness, consensus-building, and consultation.

subsubtopic: SPECIALITY CROPS-REQUEST THAT GROWERS BE INCLUDED IN AID PACKAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, farmers who grew speciality crops like mustard, peas, lentils, tomatoes, et cetera, received no assistance from the billion dollar aid package this year. Hon. Members should be aware that 900,000 acres were seeded to these crops in Saskatchewan alone last year.
The Government has indicated that speciality crop prices do not follow wheat, corn, and soya bean pricing and therefore were unaffected by the U.S. Farm Bill. However, how does it
explain the price declines of more than 30 per cent in virtually all these so-called contract crops? Yellow mustard has fallen from $15 per hundredweight to $9.50 per hundredweight; canary seed from $12 per hundredweight to $8 per hundredweight; and lentils from $22 to $16, all since the decline in grain prices precipitated by the U.S. Farm Bill.
I call upon the Government to include specialty crops in any remaining aid yet to come, the $700 million, to be fair in its allocations from now on, and to include all crops affected by the U.S. Farm Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder why the New Democrats and the Liberals have set their sights on a single target these past few days. Why are they so intent on conducting a negative opposition campaign against on the RCMP investigation into the Oerlikon affair?
Hopefully, Mr. Speaker, they are not putting up a smoke screen so that Canadians might be blind to the fact that the deficit has been declining steadily since the Conservative Party took office. Our Government has taken the necessary steps and the deficit has already been reduced by $10 billion.

The Opposition does not want Canadians to know that the Bank of Canada rate has fallen to its lowest level in 10 years or that five-year mortgage rates are down 3.5 percentage points to 10.75 per cent, a savings of $116 per month or almost $7,000 over five years on a $50,000 loan.
Employment is up, unemployment is down. The number of Canadians living below the Statistics Canada poverty line declined by over a quarter of a million people, the first such decline since 1981.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, this Government's avowed objective is to manage the country on a sound economic basis, a fact to which a number of financial institutions have been attesting all along. We have been doing very well until now, so the Opposition Parties may indeed scream and talk rubbish about any issue which strikes their fancy.

January 23, 1987
Mr. Speaker, you may rest assured that Canadians are fully aware of the significant issues on which they will cast their ballots at the next election, and we will be re-elected.

Mr. Speaker, last week opposition Members were calling for the resignation of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) for a statement which he was supposed to have made in an interview. It is the height of irresponsibility for those opposition Members to mislead the public on this matter.
The Minister, in replying to a question on whether he felt day care was the best stimulation for children, actually said: "nothing is exclusive" and "for some children, day care is the best stimulation, but one should not dismiss that for some other children the best stimulation is the parental home".
Both opposition Parties, with the support of unions, day care advocates, and feminists, are claiming that a universal day care system is needed. Yet, all across the country in our hearings many other people have come forward and said that universal day care was not the answer but that there was a need for day care and that the Government should help those who need help.
Let us not fall into the trap set by the socialists on the other side of the House who see universal day care as the cure-all for all problems. I, for one, am hopeful that the parliamentary committee, which will report at the end of March, can give the Government the necessary direction on how to treat this very crucial issue.

Mr. Speaker, the future of the Holland College Marine Centre in Summerside, Prince Edward Island, is in jeopardy because of the Government's plan to remove deck officers from the list of CEIC designated occupations for 1987-88.
This Marine Centre was built with CEIC funding some 17 years ago. Over the years it has acquired an excellent reputation with its highly qualified instructors and its up to date equipment. In 1985, 90 per cent of the students who took navigation courses obtained employment.
If accepted, the proposal would force the Marine Centre to close. This is completely unacceptable to the citizens of Prince Edward Island.
I call upon, in fact I demand the Minister to reject this misguided plan and reinstate navigation courses on the list of designated occupations for training at the institution.

subsubtopic: REDUCTION IN INTEREST RATES-EFFECT ON SENIORS' SAVINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, interest rates are falling again. The prime lending rate of chartered banks is now down to 9.25 per cent as compared with a high of 22 per cent under the former Liberal Government. That is good news because it means more people can afford to buy homes, more people can afford to buy cars, more businesses can afford to invest, and more jobs will be created.
However, for some Canadians, especially senior citizens living on their savings, falling interest rates are a worry. For them it means lower incomes at a time when taxes are increasing and the cost of living, albeit more modestly than before, is still increasing.
Seniors are worried as well by rumours that their incomes will be reduced even further by the elimination of the $1,000 investment income tax deduction. I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will bear their concerns in mind as he prepares his 1987 Budget.

subsubtopic: SALE OF CANADAIR TO BOMBARDIER-FORMER SENIOR OFFICIAL'S EMPLOYMENT BY BOMBARDIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our Party believes that Canadian taxpayers received far too little for the sell-out of Canadair to Bombardier. Now suspicion over the sale must be increased by one of the senior officials dealing with the sale, the Associate Deputy Minister of DRIE, moving to a senior position with Bombardier. subsubtopic: CLOSING OF CANADIAN EMBASSY IN HELSINKI
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government's recent decision to close the Canadian embassy in Helsinki, Finland, is a terrible blow to Finnish Canadians and a backward step for our country. It is especially unacceptable when it is being done to save money at a time when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spends millions of dollars for foreign junkets with huge entourages of his friends and cronies.
Sault Ste Marie has a large population of over 4,000 Finnish Canadians who have made a tremendous contribution to the city and to Canada. The Finnish Rest Home Association, for example, has built two excellent senior citizen housing facilities for 170 people. These Canadians are concerned about how consular services will be maintained for them with their families in Finland. Cultural ties between our two countries will be damaged by this move. Tourism will be hindered by this ill-conceived plan of the Government. Who will look after families who visit Finland in the future?
I call on the Government to rescind this order to close our Canadian embassy in Helsinki, Finland, which order is an insult to every Finnish Canadian.

subsubtopic: AWARD OF CF-5 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT MAINTENANCE CONTRACT TO BRISTOL AEROSPACE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Wednesday was a great day for Manitoba. It was announced in Winnipeg that Bristol Aerospace was awarded a $300 million contract to service a CF-5 fighter aircraft.
Speaking about the CF-5 contract, the company president of Bristol said:
It creates more business, it creates more jobs in the long haul.
More jobs and more business are important to every area of Canada. As the president of Bristol has stated, Manitoba will receive more jobs and more business as a result of the CF-5 contract. The president is confident that Bristol can win additional foreign contracts on CF-5 aircraft with the capabilities developed by his company under this contract. It is looking more and more that this contract could have a far greater benefit to Manitoba than the CF-18 contract which went to Canadair. Why all the fuss?

Mr. Speaker, as a member of the Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology, I applaud the Government's announcement in the Speech from the Throne of the creation of a Canadian space agency. The space agency will essentially be a consolidation of personnel and facilities now existing in several government Departments and agencies all of which are located in the National Capital region. Accordingly, I urge the Government to establish the space agency in the Ottawa-Hull area.
It would be costly and counterproductive to move the approximately 200 people now working here in this field to another part of the country. Hon. Members should also be aware that the Canadian space industry is located in virtually all regions of the country. A neutral management centre here in the nation's capital, free of regional favouritism, is essential to the future development and growth of a cost-effective space industry. Much of Canada's space program activity also involves participation with other countries. In my view the nation's capital is clearly the natural and most cost-effective area in which to locate the head office of the new Canadian space agency.

subsubtopic: EFFICIENCY OF CANADIAN SAWMILLING INDUSTRY-EFFECT OF EXPORT TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are being punished by the Government. Canadians are paying a 15 per cent tax on Canadian wood products because Washington wants it, and what Washington wants from this Government, it gets.
Canadians are being punished because of the inefficiency of the American sawmilling and processing industry. In terms of productivity, a Canadian worker in a sawmill in Canada averages 500,000 foot-board measure of lumber per year, but because of the inefficiency of the United States sawmilling industry an American sawmill worker averages only 300,000 foot-board measure per year.
Canadians are being punished because they are being more productive. They are being charged a 15 per cent tax not only on stumpage but on labour costs, sawmilling costs and processing costs, because of the inefficiency of the American
industry. This Government should be ashamed of itself for the way it is treating one of the main, staple resources of Canada.

I regret the derogatory insinuations in regard to the public servants made by my right hon. friend. They conveyed straightforward legal advice which I conveyed to Members of the House. I know we saw the position of the Liberal Party set out yesterday by the Hon. Member for Sudbury. You do not want the facts, you want a circus. We are here to tell you that the RCMP will conduct a full inquiry and justice will be done.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. subtopic: REQUEST THAT RCMP QUESTION ALL MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when a matter is turned over to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Commissioner and his colleagues, who command the respect of the country, investigate and set the parameters of their own inquiry. When they are satisfied that they have exhaustively analysed a matter in the interests of Canadian justice, I suppose they either report to a Crown prosecutor and lay charges or report back to the Solicitor General. It is not for me or any member of the Government to interfere in any way with the conduct of that inquiry. I allow, quite properly, the Commissioner of the RCMP to exercise his judgment, as he should.
